video.title: Fix Your Forehand Over-Rotation | 3 Counter-Rotational Balance Techniques

classification.reason: The video provides technical instruction on forehand counter-rotational braking techniques to control body rotation and avoid over-rotation through contact.

problem.title_as_question: How do you fix forehand over-rotation through contact?
problem.definition: Continuous uncontrolled twisting through the ball causes lower racket speed, loss of directional accuracy, and over-rotating off target.

quotes.text: and then I want you to look at the counter rotational break which is this left leg coming up and forward which is a rotation in the opposite direction

symptoms.description: Shots are hit slower and with less accuracy due to lack of rotation control.
Body continuously spins around through contact instead of stopping transiently on a line.
Front foot lifts or heel comes off the ground during contact rather than firmly pressing against rotation.
Feeling the front foot pressing through the ground and resisting force to prevent over-rotation.
The chest flares open excessively or the ball gets shanked off wide.

causes.statement: Player fails to execute counter-rotational breaking properly to control rotation through the hitting zone.
Hip rotation is treated as a continuous twist rather than a transient start-and-stop action.
Hips do not brake or slow down through the hitting zone, failing to create the torso whip effect.
Hitting leg does not kick back behind the body to arrest rotational spin when driving weight forward.
Left foot is not sent up or across to generate opposite rotation and counter the right hip drive.
Player fails to press through the planted front foot to generate static ground force resisting outward rotation.
Front foot or heel leaves the ground during contact instead of remaining anchored to resist rotational torque.

angles.summary: Initial hip drive followed by an opposing movement stops hip rotation through contact, causing the torso to flick through like a whip.
Roger Federer and Carlos Alcaraz routinely employ counter-rotational breaks with both legs across various forehand patterns.
MLB pitchers like Jacob deGrom plant the front leg and resist outward rotation at release, perfectly converting rotational forces into forward momentum.
A side-by-side comparison shows the front heel lifting early and rotating wide versus staying grounded through contact to control direction.
Front foot hops seen on tour do not happen during contact, but rather occur as part of the follow-through after the foot was planted.

solutions.summary: Practice driving through the right hip so that the right leg fires back behind the body while the entire body moves forward.
Train the early swing hip-driving and counter-rotational motions using a medicine ball to receive heightened kinesthetic feedback.
solutions.external_goal: Throw medicine ball using early hip drive

solutions.summary: Ensure the front foot stays planted firmly on the ground through contact and only comes up during the follow-through.
solutions.external_goal: Keep front foot grounded on the court through contact
